This is very similar to the traditional goal of verifiable computation, except that a malicious “prover” fˆ∗ is required to be stateless. In this setting, one can make a direct use of probabilistically checkable proofs (PCPs) for proving the correctness of f (x) without any additional cryptographic machinery. Using the HSS-based worst-case to average-case reduction from Theorem 23, we get checkers M with the following feature: after an input-independent polynomial-time preprocessing, any computation f (x) can be verified with an arbitrarily small inverse polynomial error by receiving just a constant number of bits from fˆ∗ . (See full version for details.) We do not know of any other approach for verifiable computation that yields such a result. 6 Conclusions and Open Problems In this work we initiate a systematic study of homomorphic secret sharing (HSS) by providing a taxonomy of HSS variants and establishing some negative results and relations with other primitives. We also present applications of HSS in cryptography and complexity theory.
